title: Cap. VIII Arg. 2 Resp.: Paul removes good and evil acts; Augustine Contra 2 Epist. Pelag.
pass_a_gloss: I answer first that they by this their argumentation directly strike against the mind and clear words of the Apostle. For Paul in this place does this, that he may teach that the election and rejection of singular persons do not hang upon diverse or contrary acts of men, but upon the diverse good pleasure of God willing to have mercy on this one, not to have mercy on that one. And for this cause he removes not only their good actions, but also their evil ones; When they had not yet been born, or had done anything good or evil. But as to those who pretend that God did not indeed regard the works which they did, but those which he foresaw they would do, and thence loved Jacob and hated Esau — since they are more perspicacious than the Apostle himself, who could not invent this response — I will not refute them, but will permit them to enjoy their dream. This only I will warn, that they patiently hear Augustine, who, irritated by this inept escape, broke forth into these words: Truly you dote, who, when the truth says, NOT OF WORKS, BUT OF HIM THAT CALLETH, you say that from future works which God foresaw he would do, Jacob was loved, etc. Against two Letters of the Pelagians, book 2, chapter 7.
pass_b_english: First reply: their argument strikes straight against Paul's mind and plain words. In this place he teaches that election and rejection of particular persons do not hang on diverse or contrary human acts, but on God's diverse good pleasure — willing to have mercy on one, not on another. For that cause he removes not only their good acts but their evil ones: when they were not yet born, nor had done anything good or evil. As for those who claim God regarded not works done but works he foresaw they would do — and so loved Jacob and hated Esau — since they are sharper than the Apostle himself, who could not invent that answer, I will not refute them; let them enjoy their dream. Only this: hear Augustine patiently. Irritated by that inept escape he broke out: You truly dote who, when truth says NOT OF WORKS BUT OF HIM THAT CALLS, say Jacob was loved from future works God foresaw he would do (Against two Letters of the Pelagians 2.7).
source_text: Respondeo primo, illos directe impingere in mentem et clara verba Apostoli hac sua argutatione. Nam Paulus id agit hoc in loco, ut doceat electionem et rejectionem personarum singularium non pendere ex diversis aut contrariis actibus hominum, sed ex diverso Dei beneplacito volentis hujus misereri, illius non misereri. Atque hanc ob causam non modo removet bonas eorum actiones, sed etiam malas; Cum nondum nati fuissent, aut aliquid boni aut mali egissent. Quod autem ad eos attinet qui obtendunt Deum non spectasse quidem opera quae fecerunt, sed quae praevidit eos facturos, atque inde dilexisse Jacobum, et odisse Esavum, cum sint ipso Apostolo perspicaciores, qui hanc responsionem excogitare non potuit, ego eos non refellam, sed suo insomnia frui permittam. Id tantum monebo, Augustinum patienter audiant, qui hoc inepto effugio irritatus in haec verba prorupit: Profecto desipitis, qui dicente veritate, NON EX OPERIBUS, SED EX VOCANTE DICTUM EST, vos dicitis, ex futuris operibus quae Deus illum facturum esse praesciebat, Jacob fuisse dilectum, etc. Contr. 2. Epist. Pelag. lib. 2, cap. 7.
